full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff instituted Money Suit No. 7 of 1956 on 31-12-56 under orders and authority of the erstwhile High Court against the respondents in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh for recovery of Rs. 99.319-13-9 and on transfer of the suit in the Court of the 1st Subordinate Judge it was renumbered as Money Suit No. 2 of 1959. The case of the plaintiff, in brief, was this. The Dass Bank Ltd. with its Head Office in Calcutta had branches at various places in undivided Bengal. By an order of the erstwhile High Court dated 26-5-1950, the Dass Bank Ltd., as respects its branches in the then East Pakistan was wound up. The High Court then appointed the Official Receiver as Official Liquidator of that Bank and authorized the Liquidator to collect debts and assets of that Bank in the then East Pakistan. The defendants who used to carry on business in Jute and other articles had their principal place of business at Bhairab Bazar in the district of Mymensingh. At Bhairab Bazar there was a branch of the Dass Bank Ltd. For the purpose of obtaining facilities from the Bank, the defendants opened an Overdraft Account in their name in the Bhairab Bazar Branch of the Bank some time in 1941. According to the contract between the parties and the system of the Bank business the defendants used to take money from the Bank and make deposits from time to time. The defendants agreed to pay compound interest with quarterly rests, at the rate of 6% per annum. The business year of the Bank was from January to December. On final account having been made, a sum of Rs. 99,319-13-9 remained as the outstanding liability of the defendants to the Bank for recovery of which the aforesaid suit was filed claiming future interest. 

 9. On the other hand Mr. S.R. Pal, learned counsel for the respondent contended that the suit was barred under Article 57 of the Limitation Act and limitation was not saved by section 73(1) of the Banking Companies Ordinance, 1962 which is prospective and as such not applicable to pending suits or appeals even by necessary implication. Learned Counsel, however, contended that sub-section (3) of section 73 provides retrospectively to a limited extent. According to the rules of interpretation, he argued, (i) procedural law is retrospective if it does not affect a vested right; (ii) unless there is an express provision, vested rights already accrued cannot be affected; (iii) the procedural law to apply to pending cases must contain something in it expressly so as to indicate clear intention of the legislature for its application to the pending cases and (iv) the date of the institution of the suit determines the law as existing on the day to apply to it. Mr. Pal in support of his contention relied upon some cases, namely, 40 Indian Appeals 74 (Lala Soni Ram Vs. Kanhaiya Lal) A.I.R. 1934 PC 77 which corresponds to 38 C.W.N. 400 (Mt. Allah Rakhi Vs. Shah Mohammad), 1875, 1 Chancery Division 48 (In re Joseph Suche & Co. Ltd.) 1898 (2 QBD 547 (In re Athlumney), 1950 (1 KB) 574 (Hutchinson Vs. Jauncey, 1950 (2 KB) 52. (Jonas Vs. Rosenberg) and A.I.R. 1955 Cal. 17252 (Jonnas Vs. Rosenberg) and A.I.R. 1955 Cal. 172 (Suburban Bank Ltd. Vs. Nistaram). In 40 Indian Appeals it was held that the law of limitation applicable to a suit or proceeding is the law in force at the date of institution of the suit or proceeding unless there is distinct provision to the contrary. In A.I.R. 1934 PC 77 there arose a question whether the Limitation (Amendment) Act, 1929 would apply or the law of Limitation which was applicable to the suit at that time would apply. The Limitation (Amendment) Act, 1929 came into force on 1st January, 1929. The suit which was the subject of the appeal before the Privy Council was brought on 29th January, 1926. The Privy Council held that the question whether it was then barred by limitation must depend on the law of limitation which was applicable to the suit at that time and not the provisions of the Amending Act. It is to be noted here that there is nothing to indicate that the Amending Act was intended to be retrospective in operation. In 1875, 1 Chancery Division 48 the Court held that as a general rule where the legislature alters the rights of parties by taking away or conferring any right of action its enactments, unless in express terms they apply to pending actions, do not affect them. It is said that there is one exception to that rule, namely, that, where enactments merely affect procedure and do not extend to rights of action, they have been held to apply to existing rights. In 1898 (2 QBD) 547 it has been held that perhaps no rule of construction is more firmly established than this that a retrospective operation is not to be given to a statute so as to impair an existing right or obligation, otherwise than as regards matter of procedure, unless that effect cannot be avoided without doing violence to the language of the enactment. If the enactment is expressed in language which is fairly capable of either interpretation, it ought to be construed as prospective only. In 1950 (1 KB) it was observed that law applicable to a case, was the law as it existed at the date of the hearing and in 1950 (2 KB) 52 it was held that the law applicable, was the law as it existed at the date of judgment. In A.I.R. 1955 Cal. 172 it was held that the suit was governed by the law in force at the time of its institution. The Amending Ordinance, 1952 was not applied retrospectively to the suit which was already barred by time under the law prevailing before the Ordinance. The cases referred to above are not free from conflict and in our view not of any help to the respondents, because the retrospectively of a particular provision of an enactment is to be gathered from the language of the enactment and the intention of legislature expressed therein.
